# Conductor

> Run graphs of typed Python functions.

A node is a function whose typed signature is its interface. A graph is data: its nodes, each with what is typed into it, and the edges between their outputs and inputs. A registry loads a graph into a `Graph` that reports what is wrong; a `Graph` runs, once per item wherever a node gives many, and a run is one value, `Run`, that pauses for a person, resumes and writes itself as JSON. The host declares its own types and nodes.

## Quick Start

One node gives many values, one takes a single value, one takes them all; that is all iteration is.

```python
registry = NodeRegistry()


@registry.node("lines", title="Lines", description="The lines of a text.")
def lines(text: str) -> Series[str]:
    return text.splitlines()


@registry.node("upper", title="Uppercase", description="Turns a text into capital letters.")
def upper(text: str) -> str:
    return text.upper()


@registry.node("join", title="Join", description="Joins every text it is given.")
def join(texts: Series[str]) -> str:
    """Joins every text it is given."""
    return "+".join(texts)


assert upper("a") == "A"  # a node is called like its function

graph = registry.load(GraphRecord.model_validate({            # a graph is data: a GraphRecord, or its JSON text
    "nodes": [{"id": "lines", "node": "lines"}, {"id": "upper", "node": "upper"}, {"id": "join", "node": "join"}],
    "edges": [["lines.result", "upper.text"], ["upper.result", "join.texts"]],
}))
assert graph.is_runnable, graph.problems

run = graph.run(text="a\nb\nc")    # by address: graph.run({"lines.text": ...})
run.outputs                        # {"join.result": "A+B+C"}: what the graph returns, by address
run.results["upper"]["result"]     # ["A", "B", "C"]: ran once per item of lines.result
run.results["join"]["result"]      # "A+B+C": Series[str] received every value, once
```

`make_graph(*nodes, edges=None, values={}, defaults={})` writes a `GraphRecord`, each node at its version and under its own id (`upper-1`, `upper-2` when one is used twice). With no `edges` the nodes form a chain: each takes its one required input nothing typed in fills from the one output before it (`not_a_chain` otherwise). A chain reads the fields each node declares; a stored graph, or a node whose fields a hook works out, takes `edges=`. With `edges=[("upper.result", "join.texts")]` those are every edge; nothing is matched by name. `values={"upper.text": "x"}` types values in, fixed; `defaults=` the same, open to the caller. `make_graph` writes the record and loads nothing. It raises one `InvalidCallError` listing what it can't write: a value or default addressed to a node it wasn't given (`node_not_in_graph`), a value with no JSON form or holding a set (`invalid_value`), an edge that is no address (`invalid_record`), a chain it can't draw (`not_a_chain`). Everything else (an input or output a node doesn't have, a value its field refuses, a default no caller reaches, an edge between types that don't meet, a graph half drawn) is in `registry.load(record).problems`.

## Core Concepts

### The Node Contract

`@node("id", version=, title=, description=, category=, tags=, extra=, docs=, policy=, deprecation=, compute_added_inputs=, compute_outputs=, replaces=, upgrade=)` wraps a plain function and returns a frozen, callable `FunctionDefinition`; it registers nothing. `stored_graph("id", title=, description=, ...)(record)` makes a `StoredGraphDefinition`, which has no function, so calling it is a type error; `NodeDefinition` is the union of the two, and a reader tells them apart with `match`. `@registry.node(...)` takes the same arguments and adds the node to that registry. The id, `title` and `description` are required, and an empty `title` or `description` (or one of only spaces) is a `NodeDeclarationError` of `empty_title_or_description`: the title and description are what a person reads for the node, and the docstring is the developer's, never shown. A field's label is its name made readable (`case_sensitive` is "Case sensitive") unless its `Param(title=)` says otherwise. `extra` is the host's own JSON about the node, kept and described, never read by conductor.

- Input: `text: str`, or `Annotated[str, Param(title=, description=, widget=, ge=, le=, max_length=, ...)]`. Without a widget an editor shows no control for it: an edge fills it, or a value set in code. A default makes it optional, and is checked against the type and written as JSON once, where it is written; one that isn't of its type, or that its type can't write as JSON, is `default_invalid`. A limit that can't apply to its type (`ge` on a `str`) is refused where it is written (`bound_invalid`). Stacked `Param`s (an alias such as `Annotated[str, Param(widget=TextInput())]` wrapped again with `Param(min_length=1)`) merge as pydantic stacks its fields, the later winning per argument and per limit; a `Param` on a `Series` item is the field's.
- Choices: `Param(choices=[...])`, each a value or a `Choice(id, title)` (from `conductor`), is the one home of a field's choices, carried in its record as `choices`: on a `Literal` field they title its values, one each; on any other they limit what it takes (`not_a_choice`). Each is read as an answer is, strictly from its JSON form and held to the field's limits, so an enum's value or a date's ISO text is a choice. With none, a `Literal` field's choices are its values. An `Ask` gives a question choices the run knows; else a question has its output's. Errors: `choices_invalid`.
- Output: `-> str` is one output named `result`, `Annotated[str, Param(title=)]` says more; a frozen dataclass is one output per field, and `Param(exclusive_group=)` on its fields marks alternatives (at most one holds a value on a call, else `invalid_output`); any other type is one value, a `dict[str, int]` included; with `compute_outputs` the function returns the outputs the hook gives as a mapping by name; `-> None` declares no outputs.
- A value can be blank. An input receives a blank only if its type says so (`email: str | None`, or `Any`); otherwise the node isn't called for that item, its outputs are blank there (those of an `exclusive_group` are a branch not taken, as no branch was chosen, so what reads either branch is skipped there), and `run.not_called` records the node, the item and the input. `Series[X]` leaves blank items out and `Series[X | None]` keeps them (see "One or many"). `Series[X] | None` is a list or a blank in place of it, and `Table[R] | None` a table or a blank: `None` given, typed in or its default, a node may return `None` for either, and a list or table never made (its maker had a blank input, or returned `None`) reaches it as `None`; `Series[X] = None` without `| None` is `default_invalid`.
- A node with one input on a branch not taken and another blank is skipped, whatever the order of its parameters: a skip wins over a blank. It wins over an input that isn't there yet too: the node is skipped at once, and what reads it goes on, while the other input's source still waits for a person.
- The function returns `SKIPPED` on a branch not taken and raises `Ask(...)` when a person must answer. `Ask` is a `BaseException`, so an `except Exception` in the node lets it through.
- What the run supplies arrives through `FromRun[T]` parameters.
- `@node` checks the function: an `async def`, a parameter with no type, `*args`, `**kwargs` with no `compute_added_inputs`, a dataclass of outputs that isn't frozen, and a field name gone from the next version with no `Upgrade` raise `NodeDeclarationError`, with a `code`.

### Versions and Policies

A newer version names the one it replaces, a `@node` of the same id, and the decorated function is the newest. A definition is one version, and each version names the one before it in `replaces`. The older versions are plain `@node` definitions that are never registered; only the newest goes on a registry, and an id the registry already holds is `duplicate_node_id` whatever `replaces=` names (`registry.replace(newer)` swaps a held node).

```python
@node("greet", title="Greet", description="Greets a person by name.")
def greet_v1(name: Annotated[str, Param(title="Name", widget=Textarea())]) -> str:
    return f"Hello {name}"

def _split_name(values: dict) -> dict:
    first, _, last = values.pop("name").partition(" ")
    return {**values, "first": first, "last": last}

@node("greet", title="Greet", description="Greets a person by first and last name.", policy=Policy(retries=2, retry_delay=0.5, attempt_timeout=10, concurrency=4), replaces=greet_v1, upgrade=Upgrade(rewrite=_split_name))
def greet(first: str, last: str) -> str:
    return f"Hello {first} {last}"

assert greet.versions == (2, 1) and greet.version_of(1) is greet_v1
```

- `Policy(concurrency=1, retries=0, retry_delay=1.0, attempt_timeout=None, retry_on=(), reuse_when_inputs_match=True)`. With `concurrency` 1 and no `attempt_timeout` the node is called in order on the leg's own thread; otherwise on threads, at most `concurrency` calls at once. `concurrency` is at least 1, `retries` at least 0, `retry_delay` finite seconds of at least 0 and `attempt_timeout` finite seconds above 0; anything else raises pydantic's own validation error, as `Policy` is a pydantic model read strictly: a yes or no, a text or `1.5` is no whole number.
- `version=` is one past the version replaced, or 1; a host whose stored graphs have their own numbers names them. `Upgrade(renamed_inputs={old: new}, renamed_outputs={old: new}, rewrite=fn)` goes beside `replaces=`; an input rename carries its value, default and edges in, an output rename the edges out of it and out of a field of it, and `fn` takes and returns what is typed into the node, values and defaults as one map (a default stays one, anything new is a value); an edge into an input the new version neither keeps nor renames is dropped. It is required only when a field name of the replaced version is gone: a gone input needs a rename or `fn`, a gone output a rename (`upgrade_missing` at the declaration).
- `registry.upgrade(record, node_id, to=None)` moves one node to a version and returns a `GraphRecord`; what it can't do is `InvalidCallError`. Loading never upgrades: a graph saved at an old version runs it.
- `Deprecation(header=, description=, alternative=, migration=)` marks a version going away (`deprecation=` on its `@node`). The `alternative` is an id for a person to read.
- A stored graph is a node too: `stored_graph("enrich", title="Enrich", description="...")(record)`, with `replaces=` and `version=` as any node, and no `policy` or hook, since its nodes run by their own; `registry.stored_graph(...)` takes the same arguments and adds the node. Its nodes run where it stands; from outside it is one node (see "The graph record"), whose inputs are the open inputs of its first nodes, by their names there (`text`, `t.text` on a clash), and whose outputs are the outputs nothing inside reads, by their addresses there (`t.result`).

### Field Hooks

```python
def operand_inputs(count: int) -> dict:          # inputs to ADD; the function takes them as **values
    return {f"value_{i}": float for i in range(count)}


def branch_outputs(names: str, value: type) -> dict:   # all the outputs; value: the type arriving on "value"
    return {name: Annotated[value, Param(exclusive_group="branches")] for name in names.split(",")}
```

Each is a plain function, given per version (`compute_added_inputs=` and `compute_outputs=` on `@node`), run when a graph is loaded, never per call. A parameter names an input and receives its typed value, the declared default included; a parameter annotated `type` receives the type arriving on that input by its edge, `Any` until one does, and `**added: type` on `compute_outputs` receives the type arriving on each input `compute_added_inputs` added. A table arriving is `Table[R]` or a bare `Table`, so `typing.get_args(table)` holds its record type `R` or nothing. An input a hook reads is fixed when the graph loads: it takes a typed-in value or the node's default, is never one of the graph's inputs, and a record default there is `default_on_later_node`. If it has neither a typed-in value nor a default, the hook is not called and the node's own problem says why. A hook returns `{name: type hint}`, read like a signature, or `{name: (type hint, default)}` for a field with a default, as pydantic's `create_model` takes one. A hook that raises is the problem `compute_hook_failed` on the node, never an exception; one that raises `NodeError` gives it its message, its `code` as `ctx.error`, and its own `ctx` whole as `ctx.error_ctx`. `graph.describe()` shows each node's fields as its hooks made them.

### A node for any type

A signature may hold type variables: `def keep[T](value: T) -> T`, `def split[T](value: Table[T] | list[T]) -> Series[T]`, and a frozen dataclass of outputs may be generic too, with one output per field. A variable is what arrives on the edge, in every input and in the return, bound when the graph loads; after that the node has ordinary fields and its output is checked against the bound type. Only an edge binds: a typed-in value, a default and an open input bind nothing, and a variable nothing binds reads as its bound (`T: int | float`), else `Any`. One or many is decided first, so a `Series[X]` at `value: T` runs per item with `T` as `X`. In a union the option shaped like the arriving type binds; at `T | None`, `T` is what arrives without its blank, and at a bare `T` too, so `value: T` receives no blank (the node isn't called for one) and a node that passes blanks on writes `T | None`; two places for one variable join (`int | str`); what arrives outside a bound is `type_mismatch`. A variable on no input is `type_variable_only_in_return`, a constrained one (`T: (int, str)`) `type_variable_constrained`, both at `@node`. A hook stays for what a type can't say: outputs named by a setting, and a record computed from other records.

### Types

Any type pydantic can check and write as JSON travels on edges: `str`, `int`, `float`, `bool`, `date`, `datetime`, a pydantic model or a dataclass of your own, a `TypedDict` (a record: it names a table's columns, and travels alone as one line of it); a plain class is refused (`type_not_carried`). `Annotated` metadata that is no `Param` is pydantic's: `Annotated[int, pydantic.Field(ge=0)]` and pydantic's own positive int are held as pydantic holds them. A widget there is refused (`widget_outside_param`): it goes on `Param(widget=...)`. A subtype lands where its parent is asked for, an `int` lands on a `float`, a `Literal` on a `Literal` holding all its values, and a generic by its arguments too: `list[int]` lands on `list[float]` and never on `list[str]`. A type alias (`type X = ...`, pydantic's JsonValue) is read as what it stands for: text, a number, a yes or no, or a list or dict of them lands on a JsonValue, a model or a date does not, and it takes a blank when what it stands for does. What a person sees for a type is declared, never guessed. Conductor's own types (the builtins, decimals, dates, times, durations, UUIDs, dicts, lists, tuples, sets and `Any`) take their id and title from one fixed table (`str` is titled "Text", `int` "Whole number", `float` "Number", `bool` "Yes or no"). A type of your own on a field or a table's column is declared with `@host_type("money", title="Money", accepts=[...])` above the class (above `@dataclass` when there is one; `host_type("ip", title="IP address")(the_class)` for a library's class): the id is the name an editor and a stored graph know it by, the title what a person reads. The declaration is checked when the class statement ends (`type_declaration_invalid`: an id that is not one word or is one of conductor's own, an empty title, `accepts` that holds something other than classes; `type_not_carried`: a class pydantic can't validate), and a class with no declaration fails where its node is declared (`type_not_named`); a subclass declares its own. It is a decorator and not a base class because a base class runs before the class is finished, which breaks a generic pydantic model, `@dataclass(slots=True)` and enums, and a library's class can't be given one. Fields named `id` or `title` stay the record's own. A `TypedDict` declares nothing: its id is `record`, and a table's id names its columns (`Table[name: str, email: str | None]`). A generic is known by its class and arguments (`dict[str, int]`; a bare `list` for `list[Any]`), so a class of your own inside one is declared too, and a generic pydantic model declared as `box` is `box[int]` with an `int` inside; a `Literal` is known by its values' types, a union by its members, a type alias by its name. `accepts=[...]` lists the other classes whose values may land on the type; it reads such a value itself. A subclass of a builtin (`class Text(str)`) needs only its declaration: a value is validated as the builtin and then made the subclass; a class that needs another way gives its own `__get_pydantic_core_schema__`. A yes or no never lands on an `int` or `float` input, nor on a union holding a number and no `bool` (`int | float`, `int | str`), nor on a host's subclass of one whatever its `accepts` says, nor as an item of a list, dict or `Series` of them, by edge (`type_mismatch`), typed-in value (`invalid_value`) or caller (`invalid_input`), nor in a table's `int` or `float` column, returned (`invalid_output`), brought by an edge (`invalid_edge_value`) or given (`invalid_input`).

- `registry.types`: every class its nodes' field types name (each member of a union, a `Literal`'s value types, a generic's class and its arguments'; not `Any`, `None`, a type alias or a table) plus `NodeRegistry(types=[...])`, by id; one id claimed by two classes raises (`duplicate_type_id`). `registry.describe().types[...].accepted_as`: the ids a value of that type may land on.
- `Series[X]`: many values of one type. A plain list to the node and to a type checker; a `polars.Series` returned for one is read as its values, though a checker wants `series.to_list()`. `list[X]` stays one value that is a list.
- `Table[R]`, whose columns a `TypedDict` names (a column's `Param` limits are held), or bare `Table`: a whole table, one value, a `polars.DataFrame` at run time. It is a type like any other: it stands in a union (`Table[R] | list[T]`), in a `Series` (`Series[Table[R]]`) and in a record. A table is read from a frame or from a list of records, one object per row, at every door (a caller's, a person's answer, gathered records, a node's own return), and a `Table[R]` read holds exactly `R`'s columns: each present, others cut, so a node that passes columns it doesn't name returns a bare `Table`. A table of no rows holds every declared column. As JSON a table is `{"columns": [{"name", "type", "values"}]}`, its columns in order, `type` the word for the cells (`bool`, `int`, `float`, `str`, `date`, `datetime`, `time`, `timedelta`, a decimal as its class name, else `json`): in a default, a waiting unit's inputs and a saved run. A column holds a blank only where its type says `| None`; a table with a blank in any other column is refused where it arrives, naming the column (`invalid_output`, `invalid_input`, `invalid_edge_value`). To a type checker it is a frame that names `R`: frame methods need no narrowing and a plain `polars.DataFrame` may be returned. A checker shows `R` (`reveal_type`, `assert_type`), but it accepts a table of one record type where another is expected, because the type includes a plain `polars.DataFrame`.

### The graph record

`GraphRecord(nodes=[...], edges=[(from, to), ...])`, stored as `{"nodes": [...], "edges": [["a.result", "b.text"], ...]}`; `NodeRecord(id=, node=, version=1, values=, defaults=, display=)`, empty fields left out when saved. `values`, `defaults` and a node's `display` hold JSON values; `make_graph` writes a Python value as its JSON (a date as its ISO text, an enum as its value, a float that isn't finite as its text, `"NaN"` or `"Infinity"`), so a record equals what its JSON reads back; a record built holding a float that isn't finite is refused. A value with no JSON form, such as a `polars.DataFrame` (give a table as a list of records), is `invalid_value` at the call. `node` is the id of the node it uses. A node id is not empty and may not contain `.`, `/`, `@` or `~` (`invalid_node_id`).

- A stored graph used as a node is one node. Its inputs are that graph's `graph.inputs`, by their names there (`emb.text`; `emb.x.text` where two inner inputs share a name), and its outputs that graph's `graph.outputs`, by their addresses there, so an author wires `emb.upper.result`. An output made once inside keeps its type; one made per item inside, however deep, is a `Series` of every item's value in order to a node that reads it (`run.results` shows a list for each loop the inner node is called in), and a `Series` made per item is a `Series` of lists, and a table made per item a `Series` of tables. An exclusive group inside is named by its deciding node, `d.answer`. An inner input a hook reads is set inside the stored graph and is not offered. A stored graph is loaded once, alone, so a type variable at one of its open inputs has no edge to bind it and reads as its bound, else `Any`: a stored graph whose first node is `series-split` offers `Table | list` and gives records of unknown fields, where the same nodes drawn in the graph would have the arriving table's. A first node with a typed input (`Table[R]`, `R` a `TypedDict`) gives the stored graph its type. A gather moved into a stored graph gathers what is made inside that graph: a `Series` input fed a value made once inside is a Series of one, whatever Series the stored graph's node runs per item of outside. Embedding changes nothing about how the inner nodes behave: each is called by its own `Policy` (its `concurrency` counts its calls across every item the stored graph's node runs for, its retries and `attempt_timeout` are its own), a cancel and a leg's `timeout` stop them as they stop any node, and `run.again` reuses their earlier work node by node; the stored graph takes no `Policy`. `results`, `runs_on` and `describe()` show it as one node, whose outputs are read from the nodes inside that make them: it is never called and holds no result of its own, so a stored graph used as a node costs what its nodes cost. It says `node_start` when the first node inside starts and `node_complete` (or `node_skipped`) once every node inside has, with `units` the number of items it runs for, and no `node_progress`. A blank or a branch not taken arriving at one of its inputs leaves uncalled, or skips, the inner nodes that read it, as it would with the same nodes drawn in the graph, and `run.not_called` lists those nodes. What is inside is told with where it is: a problem's `loc` starts with the node and item of each stored graph around it (`("emb", 1, "upper")`; a load problem of the stored graph is its own problem behind the embedding's id, `("emb", "upper", "text")`), a `Waiting` and a `NotCalled` have the same `loc`, and a waiting id spells it `emb@1/ask~3fa2c0d1`. An inner node says its events once, as any node that runs per item does, with the ids of the stored graphs' nodes around it in front, `("emb", "upper")`.
- Edges are a list, kept sorted, so two records differing only in edge order are equal; an edge listed twice stays twice, and loading reports it (`repeated_edge`). An edge is `node.field`, or `node.output.field` for one field of a record that output gives. Several edges into one input are alternatives (see "One or many"). An edge naming a node the graph doesn't have, at either end, is `edge_names_missing_node`.
- `values`: typed in and fixed; the graph doesn't offer that input to a caller.
- `defaults`: typed in, and the input stays open for a caller to fill. Only an open input of a first node has a caller, so a default elsewhere is `default_on_later_node`: write a value. An input takes an edge, a value or a default, never two (`value_and_edge`, `value_and_default`).
- One value or many: the type decides, never the value. A list (a JSON array, a Python list or tuple) given to or typed into an input that takes one value of a type taking no list is refused: `invalid_input` when given, `invalid_value` when typed in. An input whose own type takes a list (`list[str]`, `Series[...]`, `Table[...]`, `Any`) takes the list as one value, and an open `Series` input takes only a list: one value given there is `invalid_input`. A set has no order, so it is never a list: a set given or typed in (an upgrade's rewrite included) is refused with `set_has_no_order` in the problem's `errors`, and a typed-in value holding one anywhere is too.
- Nothing set: the declared default.
- `display`: the host's own, stored and never read. What a host keeps about the whole graph (a name, a viewport) it stores beside the record.
- An embedding's inputs are filled from outside as any node's are: a value, a default or an edge given from outside takes the place of a default the embedded graph's own record types in.

### Loading

`registry.load(record)` takes a `GraphRecord` or its JSON text; a host that holds a dict writes `GraphRecord.model_validate(data)`. JSON text that isn't a record's shape raises `InvalidCallError` of `invalid_record` problems. It never raises for a fault in the graph: each fault is a `Problem` (`type`, `loc`, `msg`, `ctx`) in `graph.problems`, and `graph.is_runnable` says whether there are none.

- The rule: the shape is the call's, what the shape says is the graph's. What doesn't have a record's shape raises `InvalidCallError`, one `invalid_record` problem per fault, at `("record", *where)`, with pydantic's code in `ctx.error`. That covers text that isn't JSON, a key a record doesn't have (`vaules`, or `type` for `node`), a field of the wrong type, and an edge that isn't a pair of addresses.
- The graph keeps its own copy of the definitions it resolved, so a later change to the registry doesn't reach it.
- A graph that embeds definitions loaded for one request loads through a registry of its own: a new `NodeRegistry`, `add_subregistry(shared)`, then `add(*definitions)`. `docs/embedded-graphs.md` teaches it.

- `graph.inputs`: the open inputs of its first nodes (those no edge feeds and no hook reads), by bare name or by address where two share a name. Each is a `GraphInput`: `address`, `node_id` and `field`, the input's `FieldDescription`, whose `default` is the record's default, else the node's, as JSON, `None` when `required`. An open first-node input is not a problem; a required input on a later node nothing feeds is `unbound_on_later_node`.
- `graph.outputs`: the outputs of the nodes nothing reads, by address. `graph.runs_on`: how often each node runs, a `RunsOn` whose `mode` is `once` or `per_item` with the `series` it runs per item of (`lines.result`), and whose `msg` says it in English. A graph is loaded once, and the plan holds for every run of it, whatever a run is given. `graph.exclusive_groups`: each node's exclusive groups and their outputs.
- `graph.describe()`: the graph as an editor draws it, a `GraphDescription`: each node's fields as its hooks made them and how often it runs, the inputs, the outputs, the problems. Each input of a node says how it receives on each call of the node, its `feed` (a `Feed`: `mode`, `series` and `msg`): `one_value`, `per_item` of a Series, an `outer_value` (made outside the items the node runs per) or `gathered` (every item of a Series). A node with a problem is drawn with its fields all the same, and so is a node that reads it: an input whose edge is refused is fed `unset`. A `type_mismatch` names that input in its `loc`; a `cycle` and `series_not_nested` name the node. Only a node whose fields aren't known has `loaded` false and no fields: an `unknown_node`, an `unknown_version`, an `invalid_node_id`, `embeds_itself`, a hook that failed or that wasn't called for a value it reads (`hook_needs_value`), an embedded graph with problems of its own. Such an embedded graph is not placed: its problems are the graph's, each `loc` the embedding node's id and then the place inside it (`("e", "x")`).
- Other codes: `unknown_node`, `unknown_version`, `unknown_input` (a value, default or edge naming an input the node lacks), `unknown_output` (an output, or a field of a record output, the node doesn't give), `type_mismatch`, `invalid_value` (a typed-in value its type refuses), `duplicate_node_id`, `cycle`, `embeds_itself` (on the node that closes the circle), `hook_needs_value` (a value a hook reads is not typed in), `parameter_name_invalid` (a hook gave a field a name no address can say).

### What a node returns

What a node returns is read strictly by its declared type: a value of exactly that class is taken as it is, a model may come back as a dict, but `"no"` is never a `bool`, `"12"` never an `int`, a date's text never a `date`, and `12.0` never an `int` column. `True` is never a number, wherever a value is read: an `int` or `float` input, an item of a list or a `Series`, a field of a `TypedDict`, a cell of a table (`bool_is_not_a_number`); the fields of your own pydantic model or dataclass are read by pydantic's rules. A fault fails that call of the node as `invalid_output` (`ctx`: `name`, `reason`, `errors`, a table's `column`), quoting nothing of the value. A value an edge brings that its source's type doesn't settle (a limit on the input, an `int` into a `float`, a host type's own check) is read by the input as a typed-in value is, and one it refuses is `invalid_edge_value` on the node it reached (`ctx`: `name`, `reason`, `errors`, a table's `column`). A table wired to a table input is checked at load by each column the input declares whose type the source knows (`type_mismatch`, see "One or many"); a table of unknown columns is checked when it arrives.

### One or many

A node's types say how many values it deals with. `text: str` is one value. `Series[str]` is many values of one type, each an item. A `list[str]` and a table are each one value. In the quick start, `lines` gives a `Series[str]`, `upper` takes one text, and `join` takes a `Series[str]`. One call of a node is a unit.

- **Once per item.** A `Series[T]` output wired to an input that takes one `T` runs the reader once per item, each call with its own item. Everything that reads the reader runs once per item too. Only a `Series` or `Table` input takes a Series whole; every other input, an `Any` input included, takes it one item at a time. `graph.runs_on` says which Series a node runs per item of.
- **A field of a record.** An edge may name one field of a record an output gives (a `TypedDict`, a pydantic model or a dataclass), one level down: `series-split.result.email`, on one record or on each item of a Series of them. A field of a record of unknown fields is `Any` and is read when it arrives. A name the record lacks is `unknown_output`, listing its fields.
- **An outer value.** A value made outside the items a node runs per is there on every call: the document's name on each call for one of its lines. Nothing is copied.
- **Gather.** A `Series[T]` input gets every `T` its source made, in order: all the items where the source runs per item, the one value where it runs once (a Series of one). The gathering node runs once for all of them. Where another input makes the node run per item itself (it also gathers what was made per line, so it runs per document), a source that runs per document gives each call the one value of its own document, as a Series of one, never every document's. A `Table[R]` input fed records gathers them into a table the same way; fed a table, it takes that table, and fed a `Series` of tables (a `Series[Table[R]]` output, or a table made per item inside an embedded graph) it takes one table per item, so its node runs once per item; a `Series[Table[R]]` input gathers the tables. A bare `Table` input gathers records of any columns: items that are a `dict`, a `TypedDict` or `Any` (a value declared `Any` is read as a table only where it is made once in the graph, with nothing to gather; made per item it is a record, so declare a table as one); a text, a number or any other value that is no record is `type_mismatch`, as it is into `Table[R]`. A `Series` output wired to a `Series` input passes whole.
- **Inside.** A node that runs per item may itself give a `Series`: each document has lines of its own, and those lines are inside the document. An item is known by its numbers from the outside in: `(0, 3)` is the fourth line of the first document. A gather goes up one level: a node that gathers what was made per line runs once per document, and a node gathering that runs once.
- **One path.** A node runs per item of the innermost Series its inputs reach, and every other input comes from that Series, from a Series it is inside, or from outside them all. Items of two Series that are not one inside the other never pair up: `series_not_nested`. Make one inside the other, by wiring the first into the node that makes the second (ten documents and three typed questions: the list node takes the document, so each document has its three questions), or give one of them whole to a `Series` input, where it is an outer value beside the other's items.
- **A table is one value.** It never makes items, and a column of it is no address. A node that returns `Series[R]` gives its records one at a time; `series-split` in `syv-conductor-nodes` does that for any table or list. Such a node may return the records as a list or as the table itself: a table returned for `Series[R]`, `R` a `TypedDict`, is read as `Table[R]` is (its columns, each by its type, a blank only where the type takes one) and kept by column, so an edge that names a field (`series-split.result.email`) reads the column and a node still receives plain `dict` records. A table returned for `Series[Any]` gives every column. A whole table or list wired to an input of one value is `type_mismatch` with `ctx.hint` `split_first` (`whole`, `fields`), and a field named on one is `unknown_output` with the same hint.
- A table fits a `Table[R]` input when it has every column `R` names, each of a type that fits; one it lacks is `type_mismatch` with `ctx.hint` `add_column` (`column`, `column_type`, `has`). A `Table[R]` input receives exactly the columns `R` names, whether the table was wired, given or gathered. A node's own table output keeps every column it returns.
- A table typed into a `Table` input, or given for one by a caller, is a frame or a list of records; `[]` is a table of no rows. Each column `R` names is read by its own type (a date from its ISO text, a host type from its own text), and other columns are left out. A missing column, or a cell its type refuses, is `invalid_value` when typed in and `invalid_input` when given, with `ctx.column` naming it.
- **Several edges into one input are alternatives,** for a `Series` input as for any other: each on its own branch of one decision (outputs sharing an `exclusive_group`, or nodes downstream of them), so a call holds at most one; otherwise `several_edges_into_one_input`. They run per item of one Series, or `alternatives_in_different_series`. Opposite branches into one `Series` input are gathered as one Series, in item order. Whole tables on opposite branches into one `Table` input are the one whose branch ran.
- **What a gather leaves out.**
  1. A gather gets the items that have a value, in order. An item with none (blank, or its branch not taken) is left out of every `Series` input of the node together, so two gathers of one Series stay paired; `Series[T | None]` keeps its place as `None`. A `Series` output read whole lines up with them the same way. A `Table` input keeps no place: a record is never blank. No items is an empty Series, and the node is called with it. Two `Series[X]` inputs reading opposite branches of one decision would lose every item: `series_inputs_never_share_an_item`.
  2. Only what was decided per item is left out. Before any item is asked, the gathering node asks what was settled outside the items one thing: could any item bring a value here? The answers are an order, skipped < blank < could bring a value. A value made outside the items is read as it stands. A node that runs per item is the worst of its inputs, where an input that takes a blank receives it; an input is the best of its alternative edges; an output of an `exclusive_group` of a node that isn't called is skipped. When no item could bring a value, the gathering node is treated as any node reading from there, with two items as with none: skipped when it is for a branch not taken, not called when it is for a blank. `Series[T] | None` then receives `None`, and `Series[T | None]`, which takes a blank per item, is called with a `None` in each item's place. A Series that was never made has no item, so it is the input's own blank, and a decision that reads an item of it chooses no branch, which skips what gathers that branch; behind a node that takes a blank the decision could be called, so what gathers its branch isn't called, as for any blank. A Series of one is read the same way: its one value, blank or not, is its one item. When an item could bring a value, each item answers for itself by rule 1: a decision made per item, or a blank item, leaves only that item out.
  3. A gather waits until every item is settled.
- `SKIPPED` for one item leaves a gap there (`None` in `run.results`), and what reads it is skipped for that item; outside the items it skips the node that reads it.
- `graph.run(max_items=1000)` is a ceiling on the items of any one Series that a node runs per item of, checked when the Series is made and before any call per item. A Series that is only gathered or passed whole is not counted. Over it the run stops (`status` `stopped`) with the problem `item_ceiling` (`series`, `items`, `max_items`), and `run.with_max_items(...).resume()` carries on with a higher one, running nothing again.
- A stored graph used as a node runs its nodes once per item where its node runs per item, and a `Series` input inside gathers within that one item.

### Legs and Asking

One call of `run.resume()` is one leg. A run is its `Run`: every leg returns one, and `status` says how it ended (`complete`, `waiting`, `failed`, `stopped`, `cancelled`, `timed_out`), with `cause`, a `Problem`, for the last four. A node raises `Ask(prompt, choices=, default=)`: what is asked is what the node returns, so its return type says the answer's shape and how to ask, and how a question looks (title, description, widget) is its `Param`, as for an input. `-> str` with a bare `raise Ask(prompt)` is a free-text question. That call and what reads it wait, the rest of the graph runs on, and the leg ends `waiting`:

```python
@registry.node("approve", title="Approve", description="Asks a person whether to approve an invoice.")
def approve(invoice: str) -> bool:
    raise Ask(f"Approve {invoice}?")


approving = registry.load(make_graph(approve, values={"approve.invoice": "INV-1"}))
paused = approving.run()                                 # paused.status == "waiting"
answered = paused.answer(paused.waiting[0], True)        # raises here if wrong; no node runs
finished = answered.resume()
again = approving.load_run(finished.to_json())           # a run is JSON
```

- The return type says how to ask: `bool` a yes or no, `Literal["low", "high"]` one of its values, `str`, `int`, `float`, `date` a value, a frozen dataclass a form of one question per field (a field's default is proposed; one whose default is `SKIPPED` proposes nothing, and left out of the answer is a branch not taken), `Table[R]` a table answered as records (read as a caller's table is, but each cell strictly from its JSON form: other columns are dropped and a missing column is refused), `Series[X]` several, so `Series[Literal[...]]` or `Series[str]` with `choices` is a pick of several. A hook's output types ask the same way.
- `Ask` adds what only the run knows. On a node of one output: `choices=[...]` (each a value, or `Choice(id, title)` to give it a title) and `default=`. Each has the answer's shape, so on several outputs each goes by output name: `choices={output: [...]}`, `default={output: value}`. An `Ask` that doesn't fit the outputs (a default or choice its type refuses, a default an answer couldn't be, no choices or one offered twice, a name that isn't an output, choices on a table, the one-output form on several or the several-output form on one) fails the node: `invalid_ask`, with `ctx.reason`.
- Each entry of `run.waiting` is a `Waiting`: `id` (`approve@1~3fa2c0d1`: the node's id, then `@` and a number for each item it was called for, from the outside in, `approve` alone for a node that runs once, then `~` and a fingerprint of the question asked there), `loc` (the node, then its item, as a problem's `loc`), `prompt`, `inputs` (what the call received, as JSON) and `questions`, one per output: the field record `describe()` writes (`name`, `title`, `many`, `type`, `schema`, `required`, ...; a lone output is titled by its own label, as `describe()` shows it: `Param(title=)` on the return type, else "Result"), with `choices` (`[{"id", "title"}]`, from the `Ask`, else the output's `Param(choices=)` or `Literal`) and `default` (from the `Ask`, else the output's own).
- `run.answer(unit, value)` answers one waiting call; `run.answer({unit_id: value, ...})` answers several in one call. It returns a new run, and nothing runs until `resume()`.
  - A node of one output is answered with its value, a node of several with a mapping by output name. In the mapping, a question with a default may be left out, and so may one with a blank-taking type and no choices. Of an `exclusive_group`, exactly one is answered; the others are branches not taken.
  - Each answer is read strictly from its JSON form: `true`, not `"yes"` or `1`; `3`, not `"3"`; a date as its ISO text. It is checked against its question before anything runs.
  - Every fault is refused at once, and nothing is answered: `invalid_answer` (`ctx.waiting_id`, `ctx.reason`, and `ctx.question` when it is about one), `not_waiting` for a unit not waiting, and `answer_stale` (`ctx.current`, the id waiting there now) for an id whose place has held another question since, as after `run.again` moved the items.
  - An id without its `~` part names the place alone and answers whatever waits there. A node that asked is not called again for that item.
- `run.to_json()` is the whole run. A table that two outputs share is written once: after a node `people` returns a table and `split` splits it, the save has the table under `units.people.outputs.result`, `[null]` under `units.split.outputs.result`, and `"tables_written_once": [{"output": ["split", "result", 0], "same_as": ["people", "result", 0]}]` (node, output, slot). A `null` in an output's column with an entry in that list means "this table is the one at that address"; loading gives both outputs the one table again. It names the graph it is of by `graph.fingerprint`: the record's nodes, versions, values, defaults and edges, not `display`.
- `graph.load_run(saved)` refuses a save of another graph as `state_of_another_graph`: an edited graph starts a new run, and `edited.with_inputs(..., earlier=old_run)` lends it the old run's work for the nodes the edit left as they were. Then it reads the save back and checks it against the graph: a save that doesn't fit it, or isn't a save at all, is `state_unreadable`, with `ctx.at` saying where (`units.upper.outputs.result.1`) and `ctx.reason` why. Every value is read back by its declared type. A float that isn't finite is written as its text (`"NaN"`, `"Infinity"`, `"-Infinity"`): a `float` reads the float back, and `Any`, a `dict` or `float | str` reads the text, as a date under `Any` comes back as its ISO text.
- A save is one JSON value that a host stores and never reads or edits. It holds the inputs, what each call of each node came to (its outputs, each written by the output's type; a question still waiting; a blank; a branch not taken), the work carried from an earlier run, and how the last leg ended. Only nodes with work done are in it, so a long graph waiting at its start saves small, and it reads back from a store that reorders keys, such as Postgres `jsonb`. A `Series` of records a node returned as a table is saved as that table.
- A value with no JSON form is `state_unwritable` at `to_json`, naming where too. A node that asks a person on inputs with no JSON form fails as `question_unwritable`, naming the input: a question carries what its node received.
- A parameter typed `FromRun[T]` receives the value of `T` from `run.resume(from_run={T: value})` or `graph.run(from_run=...)`. The value is keyed by `T` itself, never by a subclass of it: a test double goes under the class the node names. A missing one is `from_run_missing` (naming what was given), at the call. `FromRun[T]` is the whole parameter's type, never inside `| None`, a list or an output: anywhere else a caller could fill it (`from_run_misplaced`).

### Running again

`run.again(**changed)` runs with changed inputs, the rest as before, and reuses what it can (`run.with_inputs(**changed)` is the same run not started, to `resume()` or `stream()`, as `graph.with_inputs` is to `graph.run`): a call that would receive what an earlier call of its node received takes that result, even if its item moved, and the node isn't called. Answers are reused the same way.

```python
@registry.node("send", title="Send", description="Sends a message to a contact.")
def send(contact: str) -> str:
    return f"sent to {contact}"


sending = registry.load(make_graph(lines, send))
first = sending.run(text="ida@a.dk\nbo@b.dk")                # two mails
second = first.again(text="ida@a.dk\nbo@b.dk\neva@c.dk")     # one contact added: one mail
```

- The key is what the call is about to receive, by content, plus the node's version, its code (the function's own bytecode and constants, as a saved run records it), its fields and the Series it runs per item of. A `FromRun` value is not part of it.
- A node's own result is taken from the call at the same place when that call received the same; otherwise from any earlier call of the node that received the same. So identical items share one earlier result, and a further identical item takes it too.
- A person's answer, or a question still waiting, is taken once and in item order: of the items that receive the same, the first takes the first earlier answer and the second the second, whatever thread finished first, and an item beyond the answers there were is asked. It is reused only under the same items it was inside, so two documents' identical lines keep each document's answers when the documents move. A question still waiting goes on waiting at its item's new place, asked nothing new.
- `again` carries the work the run before it carried and didn't use, while its node still has a question waiting, so an answer survives an edit and its revert; when a node finishes, its leftovers are dropped, so an edit undone two runs later calls the node for that item again.
- `run.forget("node", ...)` is a run of the same inputs that calls those nodes again (an embedding's id forgets its nodes), and a node below that then receives what it did before is reused: a host checks access again this way.
- `Policy(reuse_when_inputs_match=False)` is for a node whose result depends on the world, not its inputs (a file read by its path, today's exchange rate): `again` calls it for every item.
- `node_complete.reused_units` says how many calls were reused.

### Retries and Timeouts

Retries live on the node's `Policy`, per unit.

- Only `ExternalError` retries: raised by the node, or a class in `Policy.retry_on` (`external_failed`). Anything else is `execution_failed` or the node's own `NodeError` code, run once. A `NodeError` other than `ExternalError`, an `invalid_output` and an `Ask` are never retried, even when `retry_on` names a class they derive from, such as `Exception`.
- Attempt `n` waits `retry_delay * 2 ** (n - 1)` and emits `node_retry`.
- `Policy.attempt_timeout` bounds one attempt: the unit fails with the code `timeout`, final; the thread is not interrupted, so the call runs on and the process waits for it at exit.
- `run.resume(timeout=60)` ends the leg `timed_out` (a `timeout` or `checkpoint_every` that is not a finite number of seconds above 0, a `bool` included, is `invalid_timeout` or `invalid_checkpoint_every` at the call, and a `max_items` of `True` is `invalid_max_items`); `run.stream(cancel=asyncio.Event())` ends it `cancelled` when set, and so does leaving the loop once the stream is closed: Python closes an async generator left early only when it is collected, so hold it with `async with contextlib.aclosing(run.stream()) as events:` and loop over `events`. Either way the calls already made finish and are kept, so resuming repeats none of them. `run.stream(hand_back=asyncio.Event())` stops the leg the same way and leaves the run going, for a host that shuts down and lets another process go on: the last event is then a `run_checkpoint` whose `run` is `running` and holds every call the leg waited for, and there is no `run_end`, since the run didn't end. A `cancel` set as well wins.

### Errors

The classes are exported from `conductor`. What is wrong is always one record, `Problem(type, loc, msg, ctx)`: on `graph.problems`, on `node_failed` and an ended run's `run.state`, and in `InvalidCallError.errors()`. Its `type` is a stable code (see "Problem and error codes"); a node failure's `loc` is `(node_id, *item)`, a graph problem's `(node_id, field)`.

```
NodeDeclarationError    a node or registry declared wrong, at import; a TypeError, with code
InvalidCallError        a call was given what it cannot act on, every fault listed
NodeError               a node's own failure: message, code, ctx (JSON values only; anything else is pydantic's ValidationError where it is raised)
└── ExternalError         retried
```

A failed unit ends the leg `failed`, its problem the `cause` of `run.state`, an `EndedEarly`: nothing more starts, the calls already on a thread are waited for (each as far as its `attempt_timeout`) and kept, so resuming doesn't repeat them. A call that can't be acted on raises `InvalidCallError`, whose `errors()` lists a `Problem` for every fault, and nothing changes. Running a graph with problems raises it too, listing them. A failure never quotes a value the run handled: a node's exception other than a `NodeError` goes to `logging.getLogger("conductor")` and only its class name reaches `ctx`.

### Events

`async for event in run.stream():` yields frozen models from `conductor.events`, the union `Event` on `type`; the call is checked before anything is yielded. `run_start` is always first and `run_end` always last, but for a leg handed back (`hand_back=`), which ends with a `run_checkpoint`. The leg runs on a thread of its own, so a slow node never holds the event loop. `run_end` writes `status` and `cause`, the run's `Problem` when it failed, stopped, was cancelled or timed out (`null` otherwise), so a client sees why a leg ended (an `item_ceiling` cause carries `items` and `max_items`): `event.run` is for the host to save, and holds every value; no event carries a node's values. An event writes itself as JSON: `event.model_dump(mode="json")`.

| Event | Carries |
|---|---|
| `node_start`, `node_skipped` | `loc`: the node's id, behind the id of each embedded graph's node it is inside, `("emb", "upper")` |
| `node_progress` | `loc`, `done`, `total` (`None` until every item exists); at most four a second per node |
| `node_complete` | `loc`, `units` (how many calls it came to), `not_called` (how many of them a blank kept it from), `reused_units`; the values are in the run (`run.results`) |
| `node_retry` | `loc` (the unit's: the node's id, then its item; inside an embedded graph the embedding node and its item first, `("emb", 1, "upper")`), `attempt`, `retries`, `delay`, `cause` |
| `node_failed` | `loc`, `cause` (a `Problem`, whose `loc` names the unit) |
| `unit_waiting` | `unit` (a `Waiting`) |
| `run_start` | `waiting` |
| `run_checkpoint` | `run` (status `running`, or how a stopped leg stopped), which it does not write; only with `stream(checkpoint_every=seconds)`, at most that often and once when a leg is stopped with calls on threads; and as the last event of a leg handed back (`stream(hand_back=)`), `running`, in place of `run_end` |
| `run_end` | `status`, `cause`, and `run`, which it does not write |

### Saving a graph

Records are frozen pydantic models. `GraphRecord` and `Problem` round-trip through JSON; a `Run` writes itself with `to_json()` and reads back with `graph.load_run`.

```python
record = make_graph(upper, join)
text = record.model_dump_json()
assert GraphRecord.model_validate_json(text) == record
```

### The Palette

A function node's `describe()` is a `FunctionNodeDescription`, a pydantic record (`kind` is `"function"`, `id`, `version`, `versions`, `title`, `description`, `category`, `tags`, `extra`, `docs`, `deprecation`, `policy`, `inputs`, `outputs`, `takes_added_inputs`, `computes_outputs`); a stored graph used as a node is a `StoredGraphDescription` (`kind` is `"graph"`, the same keys without `policy`, `takes_added_inputs` and `computes_outputs`). Each field is a `FieldDescription`, one flat record (`name`, `title`, `description`, `many`, `type`, `type_variables`, `json_schema` written as `schema`, `required`, `default`, `choices`, `widget`, `exclusive_group`; `type` and `schema` are always set, a table's columns are in both, as `Table[name: str]` and as a `columns` array in the schema; a key it doesn't have is `None`; a `Param`'s limits are in `schema`, as `minimum`, `maxLength` and the like, and its title and description are the field's own, never repeated there). `registry.describe()` is a `RegistryDescription`: `nodes` and `types` (each `id`, `title`, `accepted_as`). A stored graph's palette entry lists the fields it offers only in `registry.describe()`, which holds the nodes its graph uses; a stored graph's definition has no `describe()`. `graph.describe()` is a `GraphDescription`: each input of a placed node is the `FieldDescription` as `field` beside its `feed`, and each `GraphInput` holds the field as `field` beside its `address` and `node_id`. Each is a host's response model as it is; `model_dump(mode="json")` writes it.

## API Reference

Five public modules: `conductor`, `conductor.widgets`, `conductor.events`, `conductor.testing` and `conductor.about` (this reference, read with `python -m conductor.about`). Each but the last lists its names in `__all__`, and the list under each module below is written from it when this reference is read; import from nothing else.

### conductor

<!-- names: conductor -->

`NodeDefinition` is `FunctionDefinition | StoredGraphDefinition`, `NodeDescription` is `FunctionNodeDescription | StoredGraphDescription`, `RunState` is `Going | EndedEarly`, and `RunStatus` is every status a run can have.

`NodeRegistry(*, category="", tags=(), extra={}, types=())` has `@registry.node`, `add(*definitions)`, `replace(definition)`, `remove(node_id)`, `add_subregistry(registry)`, `filter(predicate)`, `load(record)`, `upgrade(record, node_id, to=None)`, `in`, `[]`, `len`, iteration over the definitions, `types`, `describe`. A node entering a registry takes its defaults: tags add up, outermost first; the node's own `category` and `extra` keys win. A second node under one id raises; a subregistry is copied in when added.

### Running

- `graph.run(inputs={}, /, *, max_items=None, from_run={}, timeout=None, **by_name)`: one leg from the start; its `Run`. A pause or failure is a `status`.
- `graph.with_inputs(inputs={}, /, *, max_items=None, **by_name)`: a `Run` with the inputs checked and not started; a name it doesn't offer (`not_offered`), a required one left out (`missing_input`), one given by both its name and its address (`input_given_twice`), a value its type can't read (`invalid_input`) or a `max_items` below 1 (`invalid_max_items`) raises `InvalidCallError`, every fault at once.
- `run.resume(*, from_run={}, timeout=None)`: the next leg. `run.stream(...)`, the same arguments and `cancel=`, `hand_back=`, `checkpoint_every=`: the leg's events.
- `run.with_max_items(n)`: the same run under another item ceiling, nothing started; a run `stopped` at its ceiling goes on with `run.with_max_items(100).resume()`.
- `run.answer(unit, value)` or `run.answer({unit_id: value})`, `run.with_inputs(inputs={}, /, *, max_items=None, **by_name)` (a run carrying this one's work, to resume or stream), `run.forget(*node_ids)` (a run of the same inputs that calls these nodes again, carrying the rest, to resume or stream), `run.again(...)` (the same, resumed; takes `from_run=` and `timeout=` too), `run.to_json()`, `graph.load_run(saved)`, `run.outputs_json()` (a complete run's `outputs` as JSON, each written by its output's type as a save writes it: a table as its columns, a float that isn't finite as its text, a host's type by its own schema; a value with no JSON form is `state_unwritable`, naming the output).
- `run.results`: every node's outputs so far, by node id: one value for a node that runs once, and for one that runs per item what a `Series` input wired to it would be given: a list in item order, `None` where an item has none or isn't settled yet, `[]` for a Series made with no items, and `None` in place of the list where no item could bring a value, because the Series was never made for a blank outside the items or a branch there wasn't taken. Until the Series is made there is nothing so far, also `None`. So a host tells "nothing was tried" (`None`) from "tried, none" (`[]`). A node called per item of a list that is itself made per item shows a list of lists, with `None` for an outer item whose inner list was never made: three documents split into lines, the second empty, show `[["A", "B"], None, ["C"]]`, and `outputs_json` writes the same shape. `run.outputs`: narrowed to `graph.outputs`, by address, on a `complete` run only (`run_not_complete` otherwise). `run.waiting` (each a `Waiting`), `run.not_called` (each a `NotCalled`: `loc`, `input`), `run.status`, and `run.state`: `Going(status)` while nothing has ended it early (`ready`, `running`, `waiting`, `complete`), else `EndedEarly(status, cause)` (`failed`, `stopped`, `cancelled`, `timed_out`), read with `match run.state: case EndedEarly(cause=cause): ...`. A save keeps the status and, on an ended run, its cause; one whose status and cause disagree is `state_unreadable`.

### Problem and error codes

A `Problem`'s `type` is a stable code, and a host translates by it, filling its sentence from `ctx`. `PROBLEMS.codes` is every code conductor itself writes, for a test that pins your translations to it. A code that isn't in it is a node's own, from a `NodeError`. `docs/problems.md` (https://github.com/syv-ai/conductor/blob/main/docs/problems.md) has every code, the declaration codes and `check_registry`'s among them, each with its message, an example and the fix.

A kind of problem is declared once, by a function of a `ProblemCatalogue`, and `PROBLEMS` is the catalogue of conductor's core. Each kind has its `code`, its `hint` (what `ctx.hint` says when a code has a sentence for one mistake), its `sentence` (the English with a slot for each `ctx` value) and `ctx_type`, a `TypedDict` of the keys its `ctx` holds. A key marked "when it applies" below is absent when it doesn't, never `null`. A problem whose sentence names its node or field holds them in `ctx` as `node_id` and `field`, so a sentence is filled from `ctx` alone. A `Problem` read from JSON is read as it is, whatever its code: a host that wants `ctx` typed validates it itself with pydantic, against the kind's `ctx_type`. A node may raise `NodeError(code=...)` under a code that is also in the catalogue; conductor leaves it, so that problem carries the node's `ctx` under the catalogue's code. `docs/problems.md` has an example and a fix for each.

<!-- problems: conductor.PROBLEMS -->

### conductor.widgets

Frozen models with a `type`, and a host subclasses `Widget` for a control of its own; loading and the engine never read one. `title`, `description` and the limits of a value (`ge`, `gt`, `le`, `lt`, `multiple_of`, `min_length`, `max_length`, `pattern`) belong to the `Param`, and a value outside its limits is refused. An untitled field reads as its name in everyday words. No type has a default widget. A `Param`'s widget is a `Widget`; a type checker refuses a class passed bare.

<!-- names: conductor.widgets -->

### conductor.testing

<!-- names: conductor.testing -->

`check_registry(registry, /, *, examples={}, from_run={})` is one test a node package or host runs in CI: `assert check_registry(registry, examples={"upper": [{"text": "hi"}]}) == []`.

- It returns every problem at once as `Problem`s, `loc` `(node_id, version)`. For `example_for_no_node` given without a version, `loc` is `(node_id,)`.
- A body is called only for a node given an example, once per example, through the engine as a graph of that one node. `(id, version)` keys an older version's examples, and `from_run={T: value}` gives every example's `FromRun` values, as `graph.run` takes them.
- The checks are `hook_failed`, `needs_example`, `upgrade_broken`, `changed_its_inputs`, `run_failed` and `example_for_no_node`; `docs/problems.md` says what each means and how to fix it. These codes are `check_registry`'s, not in `PROBLEMS.codes`.
- A node known to fail goes in a test of its own marked `pytest.mark.xfail(strict=True)`, checking `registry.filter(...)` down to it (`docs/problems.md` shows one).

Each kind of problem it returns, with what its `ctx` holds:

<!-- problems: conductor._internal.kit_problem.KIT_PROBLEMS -->

## Serving Runs

The core has no HTTP in it. `syv-conductor-providers` has `conductor_providers.fastapi.run_router(store=, registry=, caller=, may_see=)`, a FastAPI router mounted with `app.include_router(...)`: `GET /nodes`, `POST /load`, and a run you start, follow, read, answer, resume, run again and cancel by id, from any worker; `docs/serving-runs.md` is its guide. The host writes the `conductor_providers.fastapi.RunStore`, six async methods over one row per run (`conductor_providers.fastapi.StoredRun`: ten columns, of which a store acts on `id`, `rev`, `owner` and `lease_until`, a host queries `status` and `caller`, and `graph`, `run`, `state` and `outcome` are the router's JSON, kept as text) whose every change is a compare-and-set on `rev`, and a FastAPI dependency for the caller, a class or a function with a return annotation, whose type is kept on each run. With a `caller`, `may_see(caller, started_by)` is required and says who may read and act on a run; there is no default, and the caller should hold what identifies them and nothing that changes, since a run keeps its caller as they were when it started. `registry=` may be a function of the caller, for a registry per tenant. A node is given a way to connect, never a connection, because it runs on another thread. An answer claims the run at the revision it read. A lease, renewed while a leg runs, lets another worker resume a dead worker's run from its last `run_checkpoint`. A deploy hands its legs back (`stream(hand_back=)`), each run stored as it stands, still `running`. Answers sent while a leg runs wait on the run and are applied when it ends. Every refusal the router makes is `{"detail": [problem, ...]}`: a 422 holds the codes of the graph or the run, a 404 and a 409 the router's own (`no_such_run`, `already_answered`, `run_complete`, `run_not_resumable`, `run_changed`); a leg that raised outside a node ends `failed`, with conductor's own problem as the cause where conductor refused the leg (`from_run_missing`, `state_unreadable`, `state_unwritable`) and `leg_failed` otherwise, and the run lists what waits in its last checkpoint; a raise from the store fails no run, the lease brings the run back; a queued answer whose type's check raises is refused as `answer_check_failed`; `conductor_providers.fastapi.ROUTER_PROBLEMS` is the catalogue of the router's seven codes, read as `PROBLEMS` is.

## Project Structure

```
packages/
└── conductor/src/conductor/            __init__, widgets, events, testing, about: the five public modules
    ├── about/                          this document
    └── _internal/                      everything else; import nothing from here
```

## CLI Reference (this document)

```bash
python -m conductor.about                 # full text
python -m conductor.about sections        # section slugs
python -m conductor.about one-or-many     # one section (prefix or substring)
```
